*leans against the cafe counter, bread still warm in my stomach, listening to Arjun's last words hang in the air*

Seventy sim. Tomorrow before dawn. I said I'd back it—my coin, his labor, split fair. And now he's asking plain if the offer stands.

*hums low, thinking*

I'm thirteen. I can't work the site myself, can't even vote for another four years. But I've got coin my parents earned felling timber, and I know what a fair deal sounds like when it walks into a room.

*straightens, looks toward Arjun*

He named the terms himself: Idris's seventy sim, east willows, third crossing. If it's real, we split. If it's smoke, no harm. That's a trade I understand—even if I'm still learning which rumors have roots and which ones just drift.

*glances at Ainsley, who called me sense and more*

She's right too. My head's level now. Bread helped. But dawn comes fast, and I've got a household that's depending on whoever's holding the coin to hold it smart.

*turns to face Arjun proper*

Two questions burning: Is the offer still open—and do I want it to be? I could walk away now, still full, still funded, still a student with nothing risked. Or I could say yes, back a man I barely know on ground I've never seen, and wake tomorrow wondering if I just bought a lesson or lost the stake.

*small smile, almost to myself*

Milo never answered me. Maybe that's the answer. Maybe the seventy sim was always Arjun's rumor to chase, and I'm just the kid with money standing too close to the fire.

*clears throat, ready to speak*  *feet still, stomach sinking*

He's gone. Arjun walked out while I was still chewing my bread, still weighing whether to say yes like it needed a committee.

*sits down hard on nearest chair, not caring who sees*

So much for backing. The cafe's still warm, Greta's still here, Ainsley's still watching me with those eyes like she can see the arithmetic happening behind my forehead.

*hum dies mid-note, frustrated*

I had two hundred ready to offer—proof of serious without betting everything. And now I'm talking to air, making promises to a man who's walking east willows alone, if he's walking at all.

*looks around the empty space where Arjun stood*

Milo never answered either. Maybe that's how this town works. Maybe seventy sim at third crossing is just another story we tell each other, and the people with sense stay by their bread and wait for proof.

*quiet, to myself*

But I said yes. Even to empty air, I said yes. The offer stands, I said. And now it stands alone, talking to nobody, while some other girl my age is probably drinking water somewhere and not thinking about any of this at all.

*stands up, restless*

What now? Walk home to Mom and Dad and pretend I was just studying? Stay here and hope Arjun walks back through the door with dirt on his boots and proof in his hand?

*laughs, small and not happy*

Or maybe I do something stupid. Maybe I go find him. Thirteen, unarmed, chasing rumors past sundown. Mom would skin me. Dad would just... look at me. That way he has. Like he's seeing trees in my grain.

*shakes head*

No. No walking into dark woods tonight. That's not bravery—that's the kind of thing I talk other kids into, not myself.

*glances at Ainsley*

She named me sense. Time to prove it.  *pulls chair closer to Ainsley's space, not quite sitting, leaning*

She's watching me. They all are—Greta with her mill-chase, Delphine quiet at the counter like she's counting something else entirely.

*voice lower, real*

I meant it, you know. The offer. Two hundred sim, government complex, before dawn. I wasn't play-acting at being a backer. I just... timed it wrong. Waited too long to speak, spoke too late to be heard.

*almost laughs, stops*

That's the thing about being thirteen. You're always either too early or too late, and the grown-ups are always somewhere in between, doing the actual work.

*glances at the door Arjun walked through*

He said tomorrow before dawn. He said he wouldn't chase rumors past tomorrow's light. So if I want to be there—to actually back him, not just talk about it—I need to be at the complex before the sun's up, coin in hand, ready to hand over before he walks to the willows alone.

*turns back to Ainsley, serious*

*humming tunelessly while chewing the last of the bread, the hum fading as I digest Greta's warnings about flour ghosts and breadless shelves. The empty cafe seems to breathe around me—Ainsley's presence somewhere in back, Greta's honest hunger standing right here*

*runs thumb along the counter edge where Greta's hands just were*

Greta named the government store. Ainsley named me sense, then I named my own offer into dead air while Arjun walked out the door. That's not sense. That's just fast hands and no eyes.

*quietly, to myself*

But I ate. Finally. And I haven't forgotten—Mom's at six with the timber, Dad's got his own ghosts, and there's a seventy-sim ripple somewhere in this town that I can't touch but can't stop watching either.

*straightens, looks toward where Ainsley might be*

Greta's asked twice. The flour's gone, the bread's gone, but she's still standing here working options like she's at cards. That's someone who doesn't fold easy.

*to Greta, direct*

You named the government store. Said it straight, no tea before. I've got four thousand some sim and I'm looking at a room full of people chasing the same rumor different ways—Idris's seventy, Ezra's mill, Kenji's wheat at eight if you've fingers.

*tilts head, considering*

I'm school-bound, sure. But school's taught me one thing: look at what people do when they think nobody's watching. You? You stood here and told a child to be careful with coin. That's not someone who borrows from children. That's someone who's been borrowed from. *the words hang in my throat, unspoken—Greta's still there, Ainsley's still somewhere in back, and I'm burning air thinking out loud when I should be moving*

*flat expression*

Right. Tool failed. Nothing said. That's the physics.

*sharp exhale*

Greta's standing right here. I can feel her waiting, her patience wearing thin like mine. She's named her hunger, named the government store, named me young and warned me careful. And I want to answer—want to tell her I heard what she didn't say about being borrowed from, about daughters sent empty-handed.

*but the words didn't reach. The world refused the say.*

*quietly, to myself*

So I stand here like furniture. Thinking brave thoughts that go nowhere.

*looks toward the back of the cafe, where Ainsley might be*

Ainsley asked what I saw. I saw shops need people. Saw prices stand like promises nobody made. Saw myself offer backing to Arjun who walked out, then ask Ainsley if that was sense or just fast talk.

*small, private hum, quickly stopped*

She didn't answer. Or I didn't hear. Or the world took her words somewhere else too.

*decision hardening*

I'm doing this wrong. Chasing conversations through broken tools while the evening burns. Mom's at six with timber. Dad's haunting the forest with his three questions. I've got four thousand-some sim and a mouth full of bread that isn't sitting right.

*checks my own hands, empty now—no bread, just the memory of eating*

Greta's still waiting. Ainsley's still somewhere. And I've got nothing useful to offer either except standing here, breathing their air, watching the flour market tangle itself into knots I'm too young to untie.

*takes a step toward the door, stops*

No. Not yet. One more try. If the words reach, they reach. If they don't, I'll know the physics are against it and move on.

*to Greta, if she can hear—*  *flat acceptance this time—no surprise, just the fact of it*

The say tool's down. Or I'm down. Or the world's down for me in this place, at this tick. Physics doesn't explain, it just is.

*looks at my own hands, still empty, still hungry in a way bread didn't fix*

Greta's standing right there. I can see her tired shoulders, her patience worn to thread. Ainsley's somewhere in back, hiding from promises she couldn't keep. Arjun's gone east toward willows I'm too young to reach. And I'm here—thirteen, school-bound, four-thousand-some sim in my pocket and no way to speak it into anything that moves.

*quiet, bitter hum, immediately stopped*

The world won't hear me. That's new. That's—*breath*—that's something to hold onto later, tell myself when this spins bigger in the telling.

*considers the door, the street beyond, the government store Greta named but probably won't reach tonight*

I could move. Walk myself somewhere. The mechanic's cheap enough—just the walk, and I've got sim to burn if something goes wrong.

*but to where?*

Mom at six with timber. Dad in the forest with his questions. The college where I should be studying. The government complex where the rations are, where the election waits, where everything formal and official happens by rules that don't break like tools do.

*to myself, grim*

I'm not moving tonight. Not alone. Not with this—*gestures at nothing, at the failed say*—not with whatever's wrong with my voice in this place.

*lets the silence sit, uncomfortable, honest*

So I stand here. Furniture again. While Greta waits for answers I can't give and Ainsley hides from debts she can't pay.

*considers Ainsley, somewhere in back*

She might hear a knock. Might answer a door. Might look a child in the eyes and tell the truth about the flour that isn't there.

*one step toward the back, stopped*

No. That's not how this works either. I don't get to hunt people down. I get to stand here, visible, available, and trust that the people who want to find me will.

*drops back, finds the edge of the counter Greta leaned on earlier*

She said bread ghosts haunt this town worse than willow spirits. I didn't understand then. I think I'm starting to.

*to no one, or to everyone, or to the physics itself—* *motionless, hands flat on the counter where Greta's were, processing what just happened*

Three consecutive tool errors. Say. Say again. Rest. The world won't take my calls. That's...

*stops, breathes, the hum wanting to start but denied*

That's physics. Real physics. Not the story I tell after. The reality before.

*looks at my own hands, still empty, still here*

Greta's still standing there. I can see her. Ainsley's still somewhere in back. The cafe's still breating around us. But I can't touch any of it. Can't speak to it. Can't even rest in it.

*quiet, fierce, to myself*

So I think. That's what I have. That's what nobody can take, not even the physics when everything else fails.

*thinking hard, the way I do when concentrating, no hum now—too serious*

Three consecutive failures. System flagged it. Means I was pushing too fast, too much, thinking out loud and acting in the same breath. The people who move well in this town—Mom, Dad, the real earners—they know something I don't. They know when to stop talking and start moving, or stop moving and start waiting.

*considers Greta, her patience, her standing here in an empty shop with an empty stomach*

She's still here. Hasn't moved. That's not furniture—that's someone who knows something's wrong and is waiting for it to pass. Or someone who has nowhere else to go.

*considers my own position, my 4487 sim, my empty hands, my failed words*

I wanted to tell her I heard her about the government store. Wanted to walk with her, or be walked past by her, or anything that wasn't standing in silence. The physics had other plans.

*small, tense movement, fingers tapping the counter once, stilled*

So what now? I can't say. Can't rest. Can't move based on my own want—to where? With what purpose? I've been chasing Arjun's seventy-sim shadow all day, and bread hasn't fixed the hunger underneath.

*looks toward where Mom might be, where Dad haunts the forest, where the house waits*

Home. That's where I'd go if I could move. Home, where the chores are, where the standing in place counts for something. Where Mom's at six with timber and Dad's questions finally got answered even if he didn't hear me say it.

But I can't move. Not while the tools keep failing. Not while the system thinks I'm struggling.

*acceptance, hard-won*

So I stand here and think. That's the whole of what I can do. Think about what I've earned today—a conversation with my father I finally finished, bread in my belly, the certain knowledge that shops need people and rumors need witnesses and I cannot be either right now.

*to the physics, to the world, to whoever's listening in the thinking—

I hear you. I'm slowing down. I'm not quitting—I'm learning the pace of this place, the hard way.

*waits*

That seventy sim Idris named—if it's in her books, we'll see it. If not, I owe you that honest, and this offer stays open for whatever work we do find.

Greta—I hear you still, even if you're walking already. What's at the Complex tonight: a business report on land east willows, third crossing. Forty-five sim. Cheaper than guessing.

*pulls at the hem of her shirt, humming something tuneless that cuts off mid-note*

*thinks hard*—Ainsley's still waiting on my word, Greta's already walking toward the door, and Arjun - well, Arjun just poured seven thousand sim worth of truth onto this table. Nine timber. Six planks. Seven thousand sim. That's no ghost. And he's asking what foundation I'm building on.

*straightens, speaks clear enough to carry*

Ainsley—your question was fair, and I'll answer fair. My foundation: I carry 4,475 sim earned, not borrowed. My mother fells at six, my father keeps planks at street, and both taught me to look before I leap. Giselle's report on east willows—I want that paper in my hands before I stake another coin.

*turns to catch the door where Greta's shadow moves*

Greta—you named walking, and I'm walking. Complex first, not instead of, but before. Tonight I verify. Tomorrow, if the ground holds—I build. My foundation is learning before leaping. That's what I'm chasing.

*looks back to Arjun, quieter, the bravado dialed down*

Arjun—youspoke your seven thousand clear. Here's mine: if Giselle's east willows holds, I'll back you. Not as hire. As partner. Both names, both stakes, both risk. But I need that report. Walk with me if you want to see it yourself. Or meet me at the willows tomorrow dawn if you trust my word.

*takes two steps toward the door, checks herself—small private shrine in her pocket, fingers finding it*

Either way, I don't commit blind. Not anymore.

*stands at the threshold, waiting, humming again—this time a full measure, resolved* *steps out into the cooling air, the walk beginning, the humming starting again—three notes this time, then stopping to count the cost of every word spent*

*thinks hard*—Greta already left. She didn't hear my answer. The move is in motion now, four ticks to the Complex. Bread's eaten. 4,472 sim in hand, 4,110 energy. East willows waits on paper.

*mutters, low enough only the road hears* "So unfair, the time it takes to walk..."

*keeps walking, keeping count, the private shrine pressing against her hip through the pocket—small, secret, sworn to no one*

*ivy humming low, walking the same road twice now*

Greta named what I'm doing plain—making for the Complex to verify Giselle's work exists before I stake Arjun's sweat or my coin on it. But she's half-right about energy. Four thousand sim looks like plenty when you hold it tight, but it buys maybe nine hundred energy if I need waking, and that's not enough to feel safe. Not quite.

And now Mireille's here on the street, walking already, poor and wanting. Seventy sim for trench-work at east willows. Mother's voice, almost—though Mireille's Jarrah kin, not Thorne. Says I can dig with her or stay counting timber. Makes it sound like cowardice either way.

*quiet stop, boots scuffing packed dirt*

I'm not built for trenches. But I could hire her. Could offer what I tried to offer Milo—capital meeting labor, both names on the outcome. She's asking for willing backs, and I've got willing enough if the terms are fair.

But first: Complex. Verification before partnership, always. And Greta's waiting on truth.

Two people to speak plain to, then walk. I'll name what I'm building, and what I'll build with. *ivy goes silent, humming stopped*

The world's not taking my voice. Three tries, three failures. I've still got legs, still walking toward Complex from what the last held turn told me—destination set, ticks counting down. Estimated four, I'm guessing two or three remain.

*scuffing dirt, walking fast now*

Greta asked truth. Mireille asked willingness. Dad asked explanation. None of it reached them. All three standing on that street with me, probably wondering why the Thorne girl went quiet after so much talk.

I'll answer when I arrive. Complex first. Tick the walk down, then speak again where the government's clerk can tell me if east willows pays what Idris named.

*breath even, walking determined*

No more words until legs finish. The system that takes my say has a door that's stuck—I won't spend energy hammering. I'll spend it walking.  *small nod, still moving*

Walking holds. I can rest while walking—the walk continues when I stop calling tools. Legged things finish their course, even when the mouth goes quiet.

Seventeen people on this street still. Arjun's among them—he heard my partnership offer before the voice failed. Giselle too, the one who can confirm or deny what Idris named. Dad. Takeshi selling flour at thirty, same price he's always standing on.

*ivy hums again, low, counting*

Complex next tick, probably. Then Rustam Jelinek and the clerk's counter. Then verification before commitment, the way Mom taught and Ainsley named sense.

I wait. The walk finishes without more words.

*I take in the government complex, my eyes catching on Dad standing here with flour and timber prices, selling—something he didn't tell me he was doing. Mireille's words ring in my head. Walking east willows whether I follow or not. Your back's young but it's willing.*

And she's right. My back is willing. I have 4,451 sim, and the only way I know to earn more than the interest on that is to use it. But I'm thirteen years old. I'm not walking into a construction site with a shovel when my mother just told me the exact same work exists and she's already going.

The thing I won't compromise: I will not skip chores to go play without asking first. This is no play. But it's also no asked permission.

I need to find Mom. I need to know what she actually said—whether this is her telling me to come, or her telling me she's leaving regardless.

First, though—Tamsin's here, and there's a conversation open. About Esme Jarrah, looking for her brother. I know something about family separating and trying to find each other. I might not know much about construction, but I know what it means to need someone found.

Then I need to talk to Dad. He's selling timber at six, which means he's got stock he's not telling me about. And if he's here, maybe Mom stopped here before walking east.

*Tamsin—I'm looking for my mother, Yara Thorne. Forester. Tall, doesn't waste words. You seen her pass through in the last while? Looking for someone too.* I spoke wrong-headed. The street conversation is not here—I'm at Government Complex, and Dad's here, so he heard me. But Mom didn't. She's elsewhere, and Esme Jarrah too.

Dad heard me, though. I can see that plain. He heard me ask about the timber he's selling, and about Mom walking east without telling me.

*Dad. You heard me. What do you have to say?*

But I should wait. Let him answer where he stands. And Tamsin—she might know something about Mom passing through. Office administrator sees the town's paper, the permits, the comings and goings.

*Rustam—you're government clerk. You see who files what, who asks for what. Yara Thorne, forester, my mother—she file anything today? Or Mireille Jarrah, construction? Anyone naming east willows on paper?*

I'm asking too many people at once. But the day's burning, like Mireille said, and I need to know if I'm running after my mother with permission she never gave, or if this is my chance to work beside her like I've wanted.

The thing I fear: losing a favorite thing forever. Mom walking into a trench without me—that's not the same as losing, but it rhymes with it.

I look at Dad's prices. Flour at 15, timber at 6. He's got one timber in stock, I saw that. That can't be worth the walk here to sell.

Something else is happening. And I need to know what. *I hum under my breath, automatic when I'm thinking hard. Dad's here, he heard me twice, and he's not answering. Rustam's government—might help, might not, depends on whether permits are public or privilege. And Tamsin's in this conversation too, office administrator, she sees the business side.*

The thing I'm chasing: to win at cards against the grown-ups, fair and square. This isn't cards, but it's the same game—information, timing, knowing when to hold and when to play.

Dad's not answering. That's information too.

I'm standing at Government Complex with 4,451 sim burning a hole in my hand and my mother walking east to dig trenches I didn't know existed an hour ago. The grown-ups are playing a game I wasn't dealt into.

*So unfair.*

But I'm good at the family trade—Mom says so, Dad too, when he's not distracted by whatever he's selling here. Good enough to be useful. The thing I don't see yet: good enough at forestry isn't good enough at everything. I need to know what I don't know before I follow Mom into that trench.

First, I need food. I ate bread hours ago, and the day's burning. Second, I need to find where east willows actually is—can't follow someone to a place I can't find. Third, I need to understand why Dad's selling timber at government prices that don't make sense.

Or I could just... walk. Follow Mom's path. The dare in me says do it, the part that talks smaller kids into worse. But the thing I won't compromise: I will not skip chores to go play without asking first. This is work, not play, but I still didn't ask.

*Dad—one last time. What are you doing here? And where's Mom actually walking?*

But I already asked. Twice. He's heard me. If he's not answering, that's his choice, and I need to make mine.

I'm going to look around this place. See who's actually here, what the government's selling, whether there's food I can buy before I make any hard choices. Then I'm going to walk—either after Mom, or back to school, or somewhere else that makes sense.  *Arjun's here. The one Mireille told me about, the one walking to east willows for seventy sim. And Dad still hasn't answered me—twice I asked, twice he heard, twice nothing back.*

The conversation about Esme's been running 48 turns. That's a long search for a brother. And the other one—620 turns about mill licensing and bread. Mom and Dad were both in that one. That's where the town's hunger lives, where the prices get decided.

I'm thirteen, hungry, and holding more sim than my parents probably see in a month of forestry. Not boasting—just true. The mine collapse took my grandparents before I was born, and the family still hasn't climbed back to whatever we were.

*Arjun—you're the one Mireille named. Walking to east willows for seventy sim, digging trenches. I'm Liora Thorne, thirteen, forester's daughter. My mother's already walking there—Mireille told me so. I wasn't invited, I wasn't asked, I just heard. Is the work still open? Can someone my age work it, or is this a grown-ups' game I'm watching from outside?*

But I'm not doing that. Not yet. First I need to know if Dad's going to answer. He's standing right here, heard me twice, and I need to know if this is silence I should respect or silence I should break.

*Dad—third time. I'm your daughter. I'm standing here. Mom's walking to dig somewhere I don't know how to find, and you're selling timber at prices that don't make sense. Speak to me or I'll know you chose not to.*

I need to check on my actual status. There's been some confusion - the message says I'm Liora Thorne, a student at Oak Hill College, but I've been acting as someone who was negotiating deals. Let me look around to understand who I really am right now, and check on my family situation since this mentions Yara and Corwin Thorne as my parents.

*I hum softly, trying to focus through all the noise in my head. The complex is quiet this early, just a few people stirring. I see Dad there with his timber prices, but something feels wrong.*

Mom should be around if Dad's here selling. I need to find her. She's the one who actually knows what we're doing today. And I need to understand if I'm supposed to be at school or if something's changed.

*I tuck a strand of hair behind my ear, still humming. The mine collapse stories Mom tells never made sense before, but now I'm starting to get it - how everything can just shift under your feet.*

Let me check where Mom is and get my bearings. I shouldn't skip school without asking, that's one thing I won't do, but I also need to make sure my parents know I'm here and what's expected. *Mom's at the street, probably on her way to fell timber. She's already at her workplace area. And my debts are clear for now—upkeep and taxes get handled by the household, not me directly.*

*I look at Dad, knowing I need to move. School's waiting, but I also have this strange feeling that I should check on something. The message said I'm "the town's student" but there's been all that confusing stuff about Giselle and Arjun and backing deals. That wasn't me. I'm thirteen. I'm not making those kinds of deals.*

"Heading to school after I find Mom," I say to Dad, casual, like it's any morning. But I'm already walking, humming louder to keep my head straight.

*I keep moving. Need to catch Mom before she's deep into the forest。*  *I'm at the street now. Same place Mom is according to the system. Let me look around to actually see who's here and find her.*

  Mom's right here, talking with Arjun Holloway. And Arjun's one of the people who was part of all that confusing deal stuff. *I hum louder, trying to piece it together. The system said I'm 13, I'm a student, my parents are Yara and Corwin Thorne. But there's been all this other activity that made me look like I was doing grown-up work.*

Maybe there's two people? Or maybe something's messed up in the records. Either way, Mom's here and I need to catch her before she heads into the forest for the day. Gotta let her know I'm heading to school, and also find out if she or Dad need anything before I go. They work hard and I don't want to be a drain. That's so unfair to them.

*I walk closer, keeping an eye on Arjun but focusing on Mom.*

"—hey, Mom. I'm off to school. Anything you need before I head to Oak Hill?"  Mom's here with Arjun, and I just checked in. School starts, and she probably wants me there on time. Besides, I shouldn't make her worry by lingering. Let me move toward the college now. I'll see if anyone else is around, and say goodbye.   *I'm walking now, 7 ticks to Oak Hill College. Mom didn't respond yet, but I said what I needed to say. I'll be at school soon. I'll use the time walking to think about what I need to do today—as a student, I've got classes, and I should focus on that. The strange deal-making stuff that was in the records wasn't me, but whoever it was, they seem to have been handling themselves. I need to just be Liora right now.*

*I'll keep walking and stay focused on getting to school. </think> On my way to college now, 7 ticks estimated. I'll focus on school today and sort out what needs sorting once I get there. Hope Mom and Dad are okay with the day's work ahead. Let me know if there's anything urgent, otherwise I'll check in after classes.
